questions.key_step: Find one counterexample to symmetry: (2,3) in R but (3,2) not.
questions.justification: Direct property check on a five-pair relation with options; one familiar move. Same single-move level as 2026-P1-Q3 (L1); far easier than the counting relation 2025-P1-Q8 (L4).

questions.key_step: Check that R is reflexive and transitive but fails symmetry (no reverse pairs).
questions.justification: Routine property check on an eight-pair relation; the transitivity check is a small chain scan. One familiar move, options available. Equivalence-framed, so the +0.5 applies.

questions.key_step: Build a transitivity counterexample (BAD, CAT, KITE).
questions.justification: One standard counterexample to transitivity of 'share a common element'; no calculation. Same kind of single move as 2026-P1-Q3 (L1).

questions.key_step: S fails reflexivity at once; T passes by integer arithmetic.
questions.justification: One-move check; both relations are textbook (x-y integer). Equivalence-relation test so +0.5.

questions.key_step: Cancellation: equal union and intersection with A force B=C.
questions.justification: A single set-algebra fact applied once; options guide the choice. No close relation anchor; nearest in spirit is a one-trick L1 like 2025-P1-Q7.

questions.key_step: Spot that w=0 breaks symmetry of R, and that S is equality of fractions.
questions.justification: Two relations to judge; the zero counterexample is the one non-obvious point, chained with three-axiom checks for S. Routine chain without real insight so L2, with +0.5 for the equivalence key step.

questions.key_step: Statement-2 fails symmetry at (0,1) because alpha=0 is allowed.
questions.justification: Two statements each needing a three-axiom check, one counterexample at zero; assertion-reason format. Routine chain, level 2, +0.5 for equivalence.

questions.key_step: Similarity is an equivalence relation and (QP)^{-1}=P^{-1}Q^{-1} gives transitivity.
questions.justification: Three-axiom check on a matrix relation plus judging whether the second statement explains the first; routine but multi-step with assertion-reason subtlety. L2 with +0.5.

questions.key_step: Each element has three destinations (Y only, Z only, neither).
questions.justification: One familiar counting idea, instant with options present; 3^n for disjoint pairs is a standard pattern.

questions.key_step: n(AxB)=8 and subtract the subsets of size 0, 1, 2 from 2^8.
questions.justification: One complement count with three small binomials; the one trap is n(AxB)=8 not 6. L1.

questions.key_step: Split at $\sqrt{x}=3$ (or complete the square) and solve in $t=\sqrt{x}$.
questions.justification: One familiar move: modulus split plus a quadratic in $\sqrt{x}$, with two roots rejected against the case interval. Options available. Same flavour as 2021-P1-Q17 (L1, modulus case split).

questions.key_step: 3-digit members of $9k+r$ are $k=11..110$; sum for $B$ is $54650$, then solve for $l$.
questions.justification: Chain of routine steps (AP sums, noticing the degenerate case $l=2$ and disjointness) with a numerical answer and no options to check, so precision matters, but no insight needed. Slightly above 2023-P1-Q13 (L1) and 2021-P2-Q17 (L1) because of the chain.

questions.key_step: Class of a point under 'equal distance from $O$' is the circle through it.
questions.justification: Single recognition: equal distance gives the circle $x^2+y^2=2$. Equivalence-class topic carries the +0.5. Comparable to 2026-P1-Q3 (L1), a one-move recognition question.

questions.key_step: Use $P=I$, $P^{-1}$ and $QP$ to verify reflexive, symmetric, transitive for similarity.
questions.justification: Standard fact (similarity is an equivalence relation); three one-line checks, options allow elimination. The equivalence-relation adjustment is applied separately. Nearest anchor 2026-P1-Q3 (L1).

questions.key_step: 'None plays all three' means no common region of the three circles; check each figure.
questions.justification: One reading of the condition and a visual check of three figures; no computation. Like 2021-P2-Q17 (L1) in being a single set-theoretic idea.

questions.key_step: The class of $(4,3)$ under $ad=bc$ is $\{(4k,3k)\}$ within $\{2,\dots,30\}$.
questions.justification: Recognise $ad=bc\iff a/b=c/d$ and count multiples within bounds ($k\le 7$); small counting, options present. Equivalence class counted, so +0.5. Much lighter than 2026-P1-Q9 (L4) which counts equivalence relations.

questions.key_step: Split at $0$ and $-4$, solve three quadratics and check each root against its interval.
questions.justification: Routine three-case modulus split with simple quadratics; options available. Same type as 2021-P1-Q17 (L1) but one more case.

questions.key_step: Factor as $(x-y)(x+y)(x-3y)$ so $xRy\iff x=y$ or $x=3y$, then find counterexamples.
questions.justification: Factorisation then three property checks with explicit counterexamples; routine chain with no unfamiliar idea, so L2 before the equivalence-relation adjustment. Options allow elimination. Nearest 2025-P1-Q8 (L4) is a counting question and much harder; this sits at the easy end.

questions.key_step: $A=\{1..100\}$ from $n(n-1)\le 10000$; $B-C$ is the odd members of $B$, an AP with $d=6$.
questions.justification: Three chained routine steps (bound on $n$, parity filter, AP sum) in numerical format, so a slip in the first or last term changes the answer. No insight. Near 2021-P2-Q17 (L1) but longer.

questions.key_step: Check each statement's reflexive/symmetric/transitive claims with boundary counterexamples ($0,1,2$).

Above 2021-P1-Q17 (L1) for the number of checks, below 2024-P2-Q6 style statement sets that were rated 1 only because they were direct. Judged L2.

questions.key_step: Convert three modulus/root conditions to intervals, intersect, complement, count integers.
questions.justification: Three routine interval conversions chained with a complement and an integer count; no insight, endpoint care only. Numerical format nudges it up slightly but it stays routine, like 2026-P2-Q3 (L2).

questions.key_step: Convert both modulus sets to intervals and read each option off the number line.
questions.justification: One routine conversion to intervals, then reading four set operations from a number line; options available and no idea needed. Closest to single-move items such as 2021-P2-Q17 (L1).

questions.key_step: Find a transitivity counterexample for each relation; the one for $|a-b|\ne13$ needs the pair differing by exactly 13.
questions.justification: Reflexive/symmetric are trivial; the work is finding two transitivity counterexamples, the second of which is slightly non-obvious. Routine chain with options to check; sits at the routine-chain level of 2023-P2-Q9 (L2); +0.5 for the equivalence-relation test.

questions.key_step: Recognise 'same block of a partition' as an equivalence relation and verify the three properties.
questions.justification: Abstract wording but each property is one line; recognition of the partition-equivalence link is the only idea and it is standard. Routine chain with options, like 2023-P2-Q9 (L2); +0.5 for equivalence relation/classes.

questions.key_step: Inclusion-exclusion on sums of multiples of 2, 6, 10, 30 up to 200.
questions.justification: Standard inclusion-exclusion transferred to sums (four AP sums, one slip ruins the numerical answer). Routine, but heavier than the counting version 2021-P2-Q17 (L1), so L2.

questions.key_step: Decode $R_1-R_2$ as pairs $(p,p^n)$ with $n\ge2$ and $p^n\le50$ and count them.
questions.justification: Careful but routine enumeration of prime powers up to 50; the PDF itself slipped on the prime list, showing the precision risk, yet there is no insight. Numerical, so no option check; similar to 2021-P2-Q17 (L1) in demand plus counting care.

questions.key_step: Spot $0$ as the transitivity breaker for $ab\ge0$ and the lack of symmetry of $a\ge b$.
questions.justification: Two single-counterexample checks, each standard (zero as the breaker; $\ge$ not symmetric). One familiar move, options available; like 2026-P1-Q3 (L1); +0.5 for equivalence relation.

questions.key_step: Reflexivity forces $\alpha\equiv4\pmod7$; then the relation is $x\equiv y\pmod7$.
questions.justification: Three property checks with modular arithmetic; the reflexive condition immediately yields the option, so a shortcut exists. Routine chain with options, like 2023-P2-Q9 (L2); +0.5 for equivalence relation/classes.

questions.key_step: Count distinct products $pq\le60$ (avoid double counting $(p,q)$ and $(q,p)$) and multiply by $60$.

questions.key_step: Count subsets disjoint from $B$ ($2^4$) and subtract from $2^7$.
